lessonTitle: Explore the shades, textures and colours of a rainforest

lessonKeywords.description: how something feels or how something looks like it would feel
is where an artist adds black to a colour to darken it down
is where an artist adds white to create a lighter version of the colour
is the group of colours you choose for your artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Mixing colours creates a range of natural colours for a palette.
Blending, sponging and stippling creates different textures.
Tinting involves adding white to a colour to make it lighter, while shading involves adding black to make it darker.
Using smaller brushes allows fine details to be added to a painting.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Overmixing paint can lead to a muddy, unappealing colour, rather than a clean, rich brown.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that mixing in lots of colours makes a better brown.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore the shades and textures of a rainforest.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This lessons is all about colour mixing and creating earthy tones. Focus on the concept of balance and moderation. Encourage pupils to start with small amounts of each colour and gradually adjust. This will help them see the effects of colour mixing without overwhelming pupils with too much paint.

lessonKeywords.description: making an artwork by rubbing over a textured surface with a media to see the pattern underneath
how something feels or how something looks like it would feel
a flat, green part of a plant, often used for frottage to capture its texture

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Frottage is a technique of rubbing over textures to create art.
Different textures can be found in natural objects like leaves.
Colours can enhance the visual appeal of frottage art.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Frottage involves rubbing over textures, not drawing them. It captures the texture of surfaces rather than depicting them with lines. While leaves are commonly used, frottage can be done with various textured objects like coins or wood.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that they will need to always use leaves when creating a frottage. Pupils may think frottage involves drawing objects such as leaves.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create frottage leaf studies using different textures and colours.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to explore and touch different natural objects before starting their art. This will help them connect with the textures, shapes, and materials they are using, making the experience more engaging and meaningful. Let them describe how these objects feel, look, and smell.

lessonTitle: Artists who use the rainforest as inspiration for their artwork

lessonKeywords.description: a dense, tropical forest with diverse ecosystems
the state of being diverse; variety, especially in species or forms
how the images or elements are arranged within an artwork
a part of something that makes it special

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Rainforest themes can be identified in artworks through specific features.
Artists often draw inspiration from the vibrant colours and diverse life of the rainforest.
Artists consider composition when creating their artwork.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Explain that artists can be inspired by the rainforest without being physically present there. Clarify that art inspired by rainforests could focus on plants, landscapes, or abstract interpretations.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that artists need to have directly experienced something or physically visited somewhere to be inspired to create an artwork.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can describe how rainforest themes influence artists' work.

teacherTips.teacherTip: You could set the scene by playing rainforest-inspired sounds or music, like gentle rainfall, bird calls, and rustling leaves, while pupils work. This creates an immersive environment, helping them feel connected to the rainforest and inspiring creative ideas.

lessonTitle: Collage skills using the rainforest as inspiration

lessonKeywords.description: is an art form where various materials are combined to create a new whole
involves placing materials on top of each other to create depth in art
the feel or appearance of a surface
making an artwork by rubbing over a textured surface with a media to see the pattern underneath

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Using rubbing techniques can create different textures on paper.
Choosing when to tear or cut helps create the shapes and details needed in a collage.
Layering and overlapping adds depth and texture.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that in art, texture can also be shown visually, like drawing rough bark or smooth leaves, even if you can’t physically feel it.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that texture is only about how something feels when touched.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a collage of a rainforest plants using frottages.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Provide A3 paper for the final piece to give children plenty of space to work. Consider using coloured paper to match the theme of their creations for added effect.

lessonTitle: Draw the rainforest: studies of plants and leaves

lessonKeywords.description: a mark made by a moving point, such as a pencil or brush
shapes that have uniform measurements and do not appear in nature
shapes that do not have straight lines and are found in nature
how light or dark something is

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Using organic and geometric shapes for the basic structure creates a more accurate leaf sketch.
Different line styles can be used to improve a drawing of a leaf.
Applying tone and shading can be used to make an observational drawing more realistic.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Highlight the diversity of plant forms and individuality of shape in the lesson.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils often think that leaves are uniform in shape, when in fact rainforest leaves vary greatly in shape and size.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can observe and sketch a variety of leaves.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Weather permitting, take the children outside to gather plants and flowers from around the school grounds. If it’s not suitable to collect them outdoors, have some purchased flowers available for the children to observe and explore.

lessonKeywords.description: how the images or elements are arranged within an artwork
how something feels or how something looks like it would feel
making quick and simple drawings to show ideas or the things we see

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Arranging features of a rainforest in the foreground, middle ground, and background creates a balanced composition
Different painting techniques such as stippling, sponging and blending can create texture
Practicing with different brush sizes (small, medium, large) creates varied effects

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Demonstrate how larger brushes are best for covering big areas like the background, while smaller brushes are ideal for details like leaves, veins, or animal features. Provide examples of how different brush sizes create varied textures and effects.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils might use the same brush size for the entire painting.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can sketch a rainforest composition and apply a range of painting techniques.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Provide visual references of rainforests, focusing on textures and details like overlapping leaves, vines, and animals. Remind pupils to clean their brushes between colours and experiment with techniques like sponging for foliage or using the edge of a brush for fine lines like veins on leaves.

unitTitle: I am beautiful: drawing and mixed media

lessonKeywords.description: artistic recordings of people, usually their head and shoulders
a side view representation or view of a human head or face
the side view of a human head

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A portrait is  a picture of a person and it focuses on their face and expression.
Common features of a portrait include eyes, nose, mouth, ears and hair, chin, eyebrows, neck, shoulders.
A profile portrait is a recording of a person's face or head from a side view.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: In a true profile portrait, only one eye and one ear are typically visible, as the subject is viewed from the side.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils might think that, in a profile portrait, both eyes and ears are visible.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify the features of portraits and profile portraits.

teacherTips.teacherTip: It would be useful for students to have access to a mirror for this lesson. Alternatively, a digital device could be used for photography.

contentGuidance.contentGuidanceArea: Physical activity and equipment requiring safe use
contentGuidance.contentGuidanceDescription: Use of equipment that may require supervision for safety, e.g. scissors in KS1, needles, paint, knives, cooking.

unitTitle: I am beautiful: drawing and mixed media

lessonKeywords.description: a way to make pictures by creating them on a block, plate or screen and then pressing them onto paper
using a sharp tool to scratch a picture or design into a surface
the surface on which the design for printing is made

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A print is a picture made by pressing an inked design onto paper.
A print is created  by pressing your design onto a soft surface like foam or rubber.
A profile print is made by rolling ink onto a matrix, pressing it onto paper and lifting to reveal the profile print.
Understand that there are different printmaking techniques.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Children should be encouraged not to press too hard when engraving their design to avoid making holes in the matrix.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: You need to press down hard to engrave a design.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a print profile portrait.

teacherTips.teacherTip: For this lesson, the students can use paint or ink to create their print.

lessonKeywords.description: arranging letters and text in a way that makes them readable and visually appealing
communicating emotion, mood or energy through visual art and design
how different elements are placed and organised in a piece of art

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Learn how graphic designers use typography in posters, advertisements and everyday life.
Explore how typography can go beyond functional text to become an art form.
Create a piece of expressive typographic art that uses design elements to communicate emotion or meaning.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Typography enhances the clarity of a design, making text easier to read by arranging elements with a visual hierarchy.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Typographic designs should be minimal because otherwise they are hard to read and do not communicate a clear message.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can experiment with typography to express different emotions and ideas.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to be ambitious with their expressive typography, choosing a design concept which is meaningful to them. Provide examples such as poster designs, book covers and music albums that are inspiring to showcase different compositions.

lessonKeywords.description: the art of beautiful handwriting using specific tools and techniques
the movement of the pen or brush to create a line or mark
a decorative stroke with details added to enhance a design

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Calligraphy involves creating letters with artistic flair to make beautiful handwriting.
Learning and practicing foundational calligraphic strokes builds the skills needed to create decorative letters.
Techniques such as strokes and flourishes can help you create calligraphic letters and words.
Practising calligraphy improves fine motor skills.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Calligraphy is an art form with specific techniques, not just decorative handwriting.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Calligraphy is just decorative handwriting.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create letters using different calligraphic strokes and styles.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Where possible, provide an assortment of calligraphy materials for pupils to try, including calligraphy pens, papers nibs, inks, brush pens, and chisel-nib markers. A whiteboard may be useful for demonstrating different strokes. Encourage pupils to practise developing consistency over time.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Concrete poems use the arrangement of words to convey meaning.
The shape of a concrete poem is as important as the words used.
Concrete poems combine visual art with poetic text.
Planning is essential to effectively combine words and shapes in a concrete poem.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Concrete poems integrate text with a shape to convey meaning. They are not merely drawings decorated with words.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Concrete poems are drawings decorated with words.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can design and create a concrete poem using words and images.

teacherTips.teacherTip: This cross-curricular lesson compliments English subject material on poetry, metaphors and similes. Encourage children to create their own poems, or provide them some examples of poems written by other authors that focus on a specific object or theme that they could use to turn into a concrete poem.

unitTitle: Mark making: using drawing tools and techniques

lessonKeywords.description: using tools and media to create marks on a surface
a person who makes artwork
the feelings we have inside such as happy, excited, angry, sad or hungry

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Know that marks can tell a story or trace a journey
Know that we can use our marks to explain a feeling or emotion
Know how to recognise, identify and explore the possibilities of a range of drawing tools and drawing media

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that different styles of marks can show the emotions of the artist, such as rounded lines showing that an artist might be feeling happy and calm. The artist does not need to create an image to express an emotion.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Emotions can be shown through images but not through mark-making.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can explore a range of different marks to tell a story and express emotions

teacherTips.teacherTip: Children might want to use a range of drawing surfaces, such as large backing paper spread over tables, sketchbook paper or sticky notes to easily move around the room with.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: We can make marks using movements with our whole body, not just our hands.
Different drawing tools and media are used by artists to make marks. This is called mark-making.
We can explore using media with different drawing tools in unusual ways to create interesting marks.

teacherTips.teacherTip: For Task A, children could also create marks using chalk on the playgound, large backing paper spread on tables or sticky notes to move around the room with.

lessonKeywords.description: a repeated arrangement of shapes, colours, or lines
to use the same shape, colour, or line multiple times to create a pattern
a tool, like a small frame, that helps you focus on and choose what part of a scene you want to look at

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists can create patterns by repeating shapes and lines.
Artists can record patterns and detail in observed forms, using tools such a viewfinder to help them.
Artists can make patterns using different kinds of tools, including ones that they make themselves.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that patterns do not always have to be exactly the same each time, but they still follow a rule or idea.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Every mark or shape needs to be identical and placed in a perfectly regular sequence to make a pattern.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a range of patterns and marks using drawing tools I have made.

teacherTips.teacherTip: If using ink for Task B, a tough tray outdoors or a vertical paper surface may be helpful to allow children to explore their drawing tools.

unitTitle: Mark making: using drawing tools and techniques

lessonKeywords.description: movement is when you make something go from one place to another
an object is anything you can see or touch, like a toy, a book, or a ball
a tool or device that helps make marks by moving in different ways

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists can create marks holding a drawing tool, but they can also use objects and movement to create marks instead.
A drawing machine works by moving in different ways to make lines, shapes and marks with moving objects.
Artists might experiment with how the movement of the drawing machine creates different marks or patterns on the page.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that artists can make marks by holding a drawing tool but they can also make marks without directly touching the drawing tool.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Artists have to hold a drawing tool with their hands to make marks.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create my own drawing machine using a variety of objects.

teacherTips.teacherTip: For Task A the bouncy ball could be swapped for another object. Water can also be added to the paint to make it easier for the objects to move through.

lessonTitle: How has water been depicted by artists, makers and designers

water is a clear, wet liquid that we drink, wash with, and see in rivers, lakes, and oceans
to show or represent something through pictures, words, or actions

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists use lots of different colours to depict water.
At different times of year and different times of day, water can be different colours.
Artists can use watercolours to depict water, adding black, white and water to change the colour of their paint.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that artists can use blue to represent water, but they can use lots of other colours as well.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Artists always depict water using the colour blue.

lessonTitle: Make a collaborative mixed media collage

lessonKeywords.description: using more than one type of material to create an artwork
something that lasts for a short time and is not permanent
artworks that are much bigger than usual

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Know that artworks can be temporary and large scale.
Know that mixed media can describe artworks that use a range of materials.
Know that materials can be layered.
Understand that my ideas might be changed by others.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that some artwork can be made to be permanent, but other artwork can be made to only last a short time.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That all artwork is permanent.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can work collaboratively to make a mixed media artwork inspired by water

teacherTips.teacherTip: As this work is temporary, a photograph could be taken to record the process and the outcome in the childrens' sketchbooks. This could support the children to refer back to their ideas in later art lessons.

lessonTitle: Depicting water with watercolour and collage

lessonKeywords.description: the way something feels when you touch it
when one material is placed on top of another material
an artwork made by layering different things like paper and fabric together

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Know that texture is a word to describe how something feels
Know that artists might depict water as having many textures
Artists can layer materials to create a collage to depict the different textures of water.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that although water itself always feels wet and smooth, artists might use their materials to show the water being bubbly, smooth or rough. Artists can describe this as the texture of the water.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Artists will always depict the texture of water in the same way.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create textured papers to make a collage.

teacherTips.teacherTip: To allow time for the collage papers to dry, teachers may wish to split this lesson between a morning and afternoon, or over two days.

lessonKeywords.description: a quick, simple drawing which is not detailed or perfect
when the paper is taller than it is wide
when the paper is wider than it is tall

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: I know that light marks can be used to sketch an outline.
Artists can choose to hold their paper in a landscape or portrait position.
Oil pastel or crayons and watercolour can be used to make a wax resist artwork.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that portrait just means the paper is taller than it is wide, and landscape means it’s wider than tall. You can use both for many different kinds of pictures, not just faces or outdoor scenes.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: That portrait means the picture is always a person's face, and landscape means it can only be a big outdoor scene.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can use sketching marks and wax resist to paint water.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Wax resist works best with deeper pigments of watercolour, where contrast between two colours can be seen.

lessonTitle: Drawing: use tone and colour for facial expressions
unitTitle: Photography and painting: facial expressions in portraiture

lessonKeywords.description: how light or dark something is
an object’s appearance as a result of the way it reflects or emits light
the appearance of the face that shows feelings and emotions
is where an artist adds colour to white to create a lighter version of the colour

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Tone in art refers to the lightness or darkness of a colour.
Facial expressions reflect human emotions.
Colours can be used to convey different emotions in art.
Using tone and colour can enhance the expressiveness of a portrait.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Colours can evoke a wide range of different emotions. For example, blue might suggest calmness while red might indicate anger.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Colours are neutral and do not evoke emotion.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can use tone and colour to express emotions in portraits.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to observe how light and shadow fall on a face by using a light source and a mirror. Demonstrate blending techniques and emphasise how tone and colour work together to express emotions.

lessonTitle: Analyse a facial expression through drawing
unitTitle: Photography and painting: facial expressions in portraiture

lessonKeywords.description: A strong feeling such as happiness, sadness, or anger.
A part of the face like eyes, mouth, or nose.
To examine something in detail to understand it better.
A small part of something that adds to its overall appearance.
How big or small parts of something are compared to each other.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The position of the eyebrows, mouth and eyes helps to identify emotions.
Facial expressions convey emotions and can be captured through art.
Understanding proportions and basic shapes of the face.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There are many nuances in smiles, such as a polite smile versus a genuine smile, which can convey different feelings.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All types of smile indicate happiness in a person.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can draw and analyse facial expressions to understand emotions.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to practise drawing each of the main facial features while expressing different emotions to help build their confidence before drawing a full portrait. The “I do/we do” drawing exercises are an opportunity to practise observational skills through drawing without pressure.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Understand how facial expressions convey emotion in portraiture.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Facial expressions are a universal way to communicate emotions, even without words.

unitTitle: Photography and painting: facial expressions in portraiture

lessonKeywords.description: a painting, drawing or photograph of a person, with an emphasis on the face, personality and attributes of the sitter
a part of the face like eyes, mouth, or nose
a representation of something that is accurate and true to life
a representation of something that is more extreme or dramatic than it is usually

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Facial expressions convey emotions such as happiness, sadness, anger, and surprise.
Artists use facial features to depict different expressions in portraits.
Portraits can evoke an emotional response from the viewer.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Facial expressions can sometimes be subtle or mixed, making them challenging to identify accurately.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Only strong emotions can be seen as facial expressions.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can identify and describe different facial expressions in portraits and their emotional impact.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Consider using pictures or photos of the children’s loved ones that show clear expressions as a reference point. These familiar faces can help pupils connect emotionally and better understand how expressions convey feelings.

lessonTitle: Make your monster move - stop motion animation

lessonKeywords.description: a form of animation involving sequential photography of still objects
a sequence of drawings representing the shots planned for an animation or film
an electronic device such as a tablet, smartphone, or camera used for creating and editing animations

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Stop motion animation is used to create animations of clay models.
Stop motion animation involves taking a series of still images to create the illusion of movement.
Proper lighting ensures consistent and clear images.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind pupils that stop motion animation is created by taking individual still images. A video recording captures continuous motion. It can be created using simple and readily available devices.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that stop motion animation is the same as a video recording. They may think that you need expensive equipment to create stop motion animations.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a stop motion animation to make my monster move.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage pupils to look back at their storyboards of their monster animation. Do remember to place clay models back into an air tight container to prevent them from air drying. Try to find a free stop motion animation app to create the animation.

lessonTitle: Edit and complete a stop motion animation

lessonKeywords.description: a form of animation involving sequential photography of still objects
the process of selecting and combining shots into sequences to create a finished motion picture
saving the final version of the animation in a specific format
a single image in a sequence of images that make up an animation
when artists look at their art to see strengths and areas to improve

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Animators have to review each frame for consistency and smooth motion.
Editing frames by adding or removing images helps to improve the overall animation.
Animations can include an introduction or end page to improve the experience of the viewer.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind pupils that reviewing your work after finishing it is very important. It helps you spot any small mistakes, like jumps in the animation or unclear movements, which can make a big difference in how smooth and professional the animation looks.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that reviewing work after completing is not necessary.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can edit and complete my stop motion animation by adding final touches.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Encourage students to view their animation from an audience perspective. Have them watch their work after each editing step and ask themselves questions. This helps pupils develop a critical eye and pride in their work. Additionally, pairing students for peer review can be helpful.

lessonKeywords.description: the background or surrounding elements that add context to a sculpture
how something feels when it is touched
are ways to shape materials like clay, wood, or metal

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Different sculpting techniques such as rolling and pinching can be used to create various shapes and textures.
Joining pieces securely is essential for a sturdy sculpture.
A variety of tools can be used to create details and textures to enhance the appearance of a clay model.
Creating scenery helps to tell a story.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Addressing these misconceptions through discussion and reference to examples can help students understand the importance of scenery in clay animation and how it enhances storytelling.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils might believe that the characters are the only important part of the animation and that scenery doesn't matter. They also may believe that scenery is only for decorative purposes.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a modelling clay monster and scenery for a stop-animation.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Oil based clay works best as it will not air dry as quickly. Use air tight containers to prevent air from drying out the clay if you are retaining models between lessons. You could use real or found objects in your background. A stand can be created for your digital device using polymer clay.

lessonKeywords.description: a two-dimensional area with a defined boundary, like a circle, square, or triangle
to bring together different elements to form a whole
a small part of something that adds to its overall appearance
something that makes it special or different
how something feels when it is touched

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Identifying the shapes in different monster drawings helps us recreate them.
Arranging and combining shapes in different ways can create unique monsters.
Sketching using light lines helps mistakes to be corrected easily.
Line and texture can be used to add details to make drawings more interesting.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children of the difference between organic and geometric shapes. Organic shapes do not need to be uniform or perfect.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think the shapes they use need to be perfect or uniform when sketching.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can design a monster by drawing and using different shapes.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use the concept of sketching lightly to build confidence in the drawing process, reminding students that \"mistakes\" are part of refining their creations. As pupils add lines and textures, prompt them to think about how these details reflect their monster’s personality.

lessonKeywords.description: a series of drawings or images that are shown quickly one after another to create the illusion of movement
a sequence of drawings that represent the shots planned for a movie or animation
a quick, simple drawing that does not have many details

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Stop motion is a form of animation involving sequential photography of still objects.
Storyboarding and sketching helps in visualising and planning the sequence of events in an animation.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that storyboards are rough sketches that help plan the sequence of the animation.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that storyboards need to be perfect and spend more time on the details of the drawing as opposed to thinking about the sequence of events of their animation.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can plan a monster animation.

teacherTips.teacherTip: At this point children should have an idea of what their monster looks like. Emphasize that storyboards are meant to help them plan the sequence of events, so even simple stick figures or rough sketches are useful. Guide them to think about key moments in their animation.

lessonTitle: Sculpture: refine and finish creature creations

lessonKeywords.description: a three-dimensional piece of art made by shaping or combining materials
is a small, rough model of a sculpture used for planning
making small changes to improve a piece of art

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Using tools, paint, or additional materials to refine adds realism, texture, and character to a sculpture.
Adjust and strengthen the sculpture’s structure by securing joints and balancing weight.
Comparing your final sculpture to your maquette helps to reflect on what worked well and what could be improved.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that  it’s better to focus on key features like the face, wings, or texture, rather than decorating every part. This keeps your design clear and makes your creature stand out.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that all parts of the sculpture must be detailed.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can add finishing touches to enhance the appearance of my sculpture.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Focus on quality over quantity by guiding pupils to prioritise key details and stability in their sculptures. Allow extra time, as refining and decorating may take longer. Early finishers can move onto creating a “habitat” for their creature using additional materials.

lessonTitle: Make a tonal study of a sculpture

lessonKeywords.description: making quick and simple drawings to show ideas or the things we see
drawn marks to show areas of light and dark
how light or dark something is
mixing colours or shades together smoothly

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Tone refers to the light and dark areas of an object or artwork
Using the side of a pencil helps create smoother, softer shading
Shading in one direction ensures there are no gaps or harsh edges
Blending from light to dark creates smooth transitions and realistic tones

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Tone includes both light and dark areas, and the goal is to show the full range of tones, from light highlights to deep shadows. Using the side of the pencil for softer shading, helps to avoid harsh lines.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may believe that tone is only about making things darker and that shading should be done with harsh, straight lines.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can create a tonal study of a sculpture.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Remind students that tonal studies take time and mistakes are part of the learning process. Show a finished tonal study to clarify the task and goal. Encourage collaboration by pairing pupils to share and discuss their shading techniques for feedback.

lessonTitle: Sketchbook research: insect, animal and bird studies and designs

lessonKeywords.description: a mark made by a moving point, such as a pencil or brush
shapes that have uniform measurements and do not appear in nature
shapes that do not have straight lines and are found in nature
how light or dark something is
drawn marks to show areas of light and dark

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Using organic and geometric shapes for the basic structure creates a more accurate sketch.
Different line styles can be used to create interest in a drawing.
Applying tone and shading can be used to make an observational drawing more realistic.
Using a photograph to draw from helps you to see details and shapes clearly, making it easier to draw accurately.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Encourage pupils to cast shadows and to look at the tone of the shadow. Observe the tone on different coloured objects. Draw pupils' attention to the fact that shadows are not always black.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think that shadows are always black.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can observe and sketch insect, animal, or bird features in my sketchbook.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Use real-life references, photographs, or nature walks to observe insect, animal, and bird features.

lessonKeywords.description: is a small, rough model of a sculpture used for planning
something that has height, width, and depth - unlike a flat drawing or picture
is a skeleton for your model and a strong frame that gives shape and holds your maquette together

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: A maquette is a small three-dimensional model used by artists to plan and develop their sculptures.
Techniques for building a stable armature include creating a framework with materials like wire, card, or foil.
Sketches or photos can be used to replicate accurate proportions and shapes in a sculpture.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind pupils that a maquette is a smaller version to plan and test ideas before making a bigger sculpture. The main shape and structure need to be built first to support the details.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Pupils may think a maquette is the final sculpture and needs to be large. They may also jump into adding small details before constructing the basic form.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can construct a three-dimensional maquette of a chosen animal, bird, or insect.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Demonstrate how to create a simple armature using wire, card, or foil to provide structure, and emphasise layering lightweight materials like paper or clay to build up the form. Remind pupils to focus on key characteristics (e.g., wings, legs, or tail) to make their maquette recognisable and unique.

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Referring to a maquette helps decide the size, shape, and balance of the sculpture.

lessonKeywords.description: something which has a bend or a rounded shape
something that repeats in a regular way, like shapes, colours, or numbers
something which is round and shaped like a circle

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Know that curved lines and patterns are found in nature.
Know that a loom can be shaped like a rectangle or circular, to create weavings in different shapes.
Know that weavings can be embellished.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that some weavings are made on square or rectangular looms, but weavings do not have to be made on looms with straight sides. Looms can be curved.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: All looms are rectangular.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can take inspiration from underwater creatures to create a circular weaving.

teacherTips.teacherTip: While some children are working on Task A in their sketchbooks, groups of children could be invited to work on Task B (2). Printed images of each selected sea creature could be placed next to the circular loom, to support children with selecting shapes and patterns that they wish to include.

lessonTitle: Weaving using everyday objects as a frame

lessonKeywords.description: something that we use or see regularly in our daily lives
thin pieces of string or material, often used for sewing or making things like weavings
a tool used to carry the weft thread through the warp threads

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Artists can make looms from everyday objects and found objects.
A shuttle can be used to carry the weft threads through the warp threads.
Artists might choose to follow their design closely, or change their mind about some elements.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind children that looms can be made on a wide variety of frames, including found sticks or paper plates.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Looms cannot be made from everyday objects.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can make a weaving using an everyday object as a loom.

teacherTips.teacherTip: Teachers may wish to complete Task A in small groups, so that children can be supported with making thier looms. For some children, it may be better to pre-prepare some looms for them to choose from.

lessonKeywords.description: to add extra details or decorations to a textile
when we think about our artwork to understand how good it is and how we could make it better
sharing your ideas about other people’s artwork

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Embellishment can be added to a weaving using buttons, beads, stitch and fabric.
Know that evaluating artwork is an important part of the design process.
Know how to offer feedback to other artists, to help them improve over time.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Remind pupils that evaluation is more than just saying what we like or dislike about an artwork. It should help an artist improve their work over time.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Evaluating is only saying what you like or dislike

pupilLessonOutcome: I can embellish and evaluate my own textile artwork

teacherTips.teacherTip: Pupils might find it useful to have threads and yarn pre-cut into lengths to help them complete the sewing element. If being completed in the Autumn term, pupils could complete the embelishment in guided groups with adult support.

lessonTitle: An artist's response to plastic waste

lessonKeywords.description: anything that is unwanted or unused
a small part broken off or separated from something

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: Human beings are creating a lot of plastic pollution in the oceans.
Artists make us think and feel emotionally about their work.
We record our thoughts and feelings about artists' work in our sketchbooks.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: Art can be made from almost anything, including plastic waste, as in the case of Mandy Barker.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: Art is only made from traditional art materials.

pupilLessonOutcome: I understand how an artist has made art in response to plastic waste.
transcript_sentences:
Hello everyone.
I'm Miss Mia and I'm really excited to join you on your learning journey.
I can't wait to explore new ideas, create amazing projects, and have fun with you all as we discover and learn together.
In today's lesson, you'll be able to explain the harmful effects of plastic waste and respond to an artist's work on this theme.
Your keywords are on the screen now and I'd like you to repeat them after me.
Waste.
Fragment.
Now let's have a look at the definitions for those words.
So anything that is unwanted or unused is usually called waste.
So anything that you might not need.
A fragment is a small part broken off or separated from something.
So imagine you have a big cookie and you break off a small piece of it, that part will be known as a fragment.
So this lesson is all about artists' responses to plastic pollution.
And this lesson is made of three lesson cycles.
Our first lesson cycle is to do with the harmful effect of plastic waste and how that might be impacting us and how we also might be contributing to it.
Our second lesson cycle is then moving on to looking at Mandy Barker's response to plastic waste.

So by learning about the harmful effects of plastic waste and exploring Mandy Barker's work, I'm hoping we can better understand the importance of looking after our environment.
Let's get started.
Now, did you know, globally, 400 million metric tonnes of plastic is produced each year? That is a lot, an unimaginable amount.
Much of this goes into rivers and pollutes the ocean.
And out of this, only 9% of plastic is recycled.
That is a very small amount.
Now, how long does it take plastic waste to decompose and break down? Now we've got some items here.
A plastic bag, takeaway coffee cups, plastic straws, and plastic bottles.
A plastic bag would take 20 years to decompose.
A takeaway coffee cup takes about 30 years.
A plastic straw could take about 200 years.
And lastly, plastic bottles can take about 450 years.
So you see, different plastics can take different amounts of time to break down and then disappear into the earth.
That's why it's super important that we try do our bit to try and recycle these items. And this is why it's so important to use less plastic when possible.
Over to you, I'd like you to think about this question.

So what did you get? If you got C, you are correct.
The plastic that you use today can take between 20 and 500 years to fully decompose.

Well done if you've got that correct.
Let's move on.
Ooh, what a lovely image.

In September, 2019, 72,000 volunteers from a group called Break Free From Plastic carried out a survey to find out what plastic had washed up on the beaches.

Over to you.
True or false? Plastics in the oceans do not affect animals.

So what did you get? If you got false, you are correct.

In Henderson Island, plastic waste killed half a million crabs and volunteers found fragments of plastic containers that had been eaten by turtles, sharks, and fish.
So this often happens because animals can mistaken plastic for food and they'll eat them and they can get sick.
And then also the plastics can tangle the animals, which can eventually hurt them and potentially lead them to die.
So it's not really good.
We need to keep an eye on how much plastic we're either buying with foods or throwing away.
Onto the main task for this part of the lesson cycle.
What I'd like you to do is think about, write down or share three ways that plastic is harmful to the environment.
You can pause the video here and click play when you're ready to rejoin us.
So what did you get? Well, Lucas and Izzy shared these ways that plastic is harmful to the environment.
Lucas says, plastic waste can take hundreds of years to decompose and break down.
Izzy says, fragments of plastic are eaten by sea creatures such as turtles, sharks, and fish.

Fantastic.
Let's move on.
Now we're moving on to our second lesson cycle, and this is all about Mandy Barker's response to plastic waste.
Artist Mandy Barker travelled with the Break Free From Plastic group.
She collected plastic waste from beaches and oceans and arranged the collected items into compositions.
She created a series of photographs inspired by what she saw.
So here we have a picture of one of her creations.
And I love the way she's displayed some of the recycled items that she's seen.
Now, Mandy Barker's photographic series is called Shelf-Life.
Barker's work combines art with a strong environmental message.
Hmm, I wonder what that message might be.
Her work aims to raise awareness of environmental issues and to persuade people to act against plastic waste.
Now this is one of the images from the series Shelf-Life.

lessonTitle: Draw fossils in an abstract style

lessonKeywords.description: art that does not try to represent something realistically, but uses lines, colours and textures instead
change the position or order of something
a form which contains several different shapes combined within it

keyLearningPoints.keyLearningPoint: The complex forms we observe can be drawn by breaking them down into simpler component shapes.
Abstract art can be made by simplifying and rearranging shapes and lines to our own artistic intentions.

misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.response: There is no right or wrong - in abstract art shapes and lines can be rearranged according to the intentions of the artist.
misconceptionsAndCommonMistakes.misconception: There is a right and wrong way in which to rearrange lines and shapes when making abstract art.

pupilLessonOutcome: I can draw the simple shapes and lines of a complex fossil then rearrange them into my own abstract picture.

teacherTips.teacherTip: In Task A pupils might draw from the fossil image provided or from another fossil drawing, photographs or real life fossils.

Hello, everyone.

B, artists sometimes make art that encourages viewers to consider how their actions today might shape tomorrow.

So what did you get? You should have got B and C.
B is correct because artists often create thought-provoking pieces that reflect the present while emphasising the potential consequences of current actions on the future.
For instance, environmental artists may depict the effects of pollution, climate change, or deforestation prompting us as viewers to reflect on how their everyday choices impact the planet and its future generations.
Now, these works can function as both warnings and calls to action, urging us as individuals to consider the sustainability of our choices, whether they are related to environmental, whether they are related to environmental, social, or political matters.

By showing these problems in a new way, artists help us see how important it is to take care of earth.
They remind us to use less plastic and recycle more so we can keep the planet clean and safe for animals and people.
Through their art, they inspire us to make changes and protect the environment.
Well done if you manage to get B and C.
